Why, the right hon. gentleman knows perfectly well that one of the weapons used by Mr. Hanbury is that if Canadian cattle were admitted, the cattle of all other countries would have to be admitted on the same terms. Now in what position do we find ourselves ? It has been pointed out by my

lion, friend from Pictou, and by other gentlemen in this debate, that the question was put aside because it was not thought of sufficient importance to be taken up. Who suggested that it was not of sufficient importance ? Certainly it could not have been the Canadian delegates. It was a most natural suggestion to come from a government who has taken so arbitrary a position, and it was the duty of our Canadian delegates to protest against taking any such position. The people of Canada will regard that as a complete abandonment of our position. What was the proposition that followed ? That a better way of attaining the object would be to have a conference with Mr. Hanbury, the gentleman who had set his face against reason, against argument, against fact in his determination to exclude Canadian cattle. I say the period is past when we in Canada should feel called upon to convince the British government that there is no reason why Canadian cattle should be excluded ; the period has now arrived when the people of Canada should enter a protest against the arbitrary position taken by the British government. Mr. Hanbury is pleased to say that possibly there may be disease in Canadian herds in the future. Now there can be no more absurd position for a gentleman occupying his right rank to take as a pretext for excluding Canadian cattle. Mr. Hanbury and every other intelligent man knows that Canadian herds are free from disease, and have been for years. Now it has been pointed out by several gentlemen on this side of the House that Mr. Hanbury is adopting this course as a measure of protection to the cattle raisers of the United Kingdom. He declares himself that to admit Canadian cattle would be to destroy largely the interest of cattle growers in a portion of the United Kingdom. That is plain.
Now let us remember that the Canadian representatives at the colonial conference were prepared to abandon a question that seems to me to overshadow all others. I ask hon. gentlemen opposite if they think there is a single gentleman in this House who will contend for a moment that the question of the metric system, important as it is in itself, or the question of reduced postage upon newspapers between Canada and Great Britain, are questions that, both together, can be weighed against this question affecting the raisers of cattle in Canada. Why, the idea is absurd. We were told on a former occasion by the Minister of Customs, with a tear in his voice, that we had touched the hearts of the British people, that while we had not a legal preference we had still better preference in the hearts of the people of Great Britain ; and he instanced the case under discussion to-day and declared from his place in this House what a weapon that preference would he with which to go to the British public and ask for the removal of that unfair restriction. As I said at the beginning, I Mr. CLANCY.
merely rose to protest against the attitude of the Minister of Finance, who has given a most trivial reason for setting this question aside, namely, that the papers were not brought down. Surely those papers have been in the departments for a long time. They must be in the Department of Agriculture, or at least in some other departments where they are easily procurable. The hon. gentleman should have laid these papers on the table before this time. He did not have to get the consent of the imperial authorities before he could do so. He might well have anticipated the anxiety of the people of this country on this great question, and have been prepared to treat it on its merits rather than to take shelter behind a pretense that this motion was a want of confidence.

For a number of years, up to a period four or five years ago, I used to bring this question up annually. When I was in England in 1897 I discussed the matter with a number of prominent people there, and I found that they would not under any consideration entertain a proposition to allow Canadian cattle to enter on any better terms than they were giving us. In other words, it was a straight policy of protection to the British farmer as against Canadian and American cattle. I pointed out at that time that they cculd protect the farmers to a much better extent than by shutting out our cattle. If they examine the freight rates from almost any part of Ireland, from almost any part of Scotland and from even the midland districts of England from the large centres they will find that the freight rates on cattle to the central markets of Great Britain are almost as much as they are from parts of the United States of America to the British islands and that by looking into the regulation of their own freight rates they may protect their own farmers to a much greater extent than any injury that would accrue from allowing our cattle in. It has been said by a very eminent English statesman within recent times that British diplomacy -all diplomacy in fact-consists of personal influence, personal intrigue and personal unscrupulousness. I refer to Sir Edward Mon-son, British Ambassador at Paris. I have to say, here, that as a Canadian I do not intend, so far as I am concerned, that Great Britain shall be allowed to blacken the character of Canadian cattle by saying that tuberculosis and other diseases exist in this country merely in order to carry out their usual policy of intrigue. Let them come out and declare that they are going to protect their own farmers and it would he fair to our people if they do so. I want to point out to the Britisher that, when he taxes Canadians he should put us in all respects on an equal footing with Russians, Germans, Frenchmen, and the nations of Europe. Canada does not cost the people of Great Britain one dollar in taxes, while these

European nations impose a heavy tax on the people of Great Britain. I demand that we shall receive better treatment from Great Britain or that we shall find out the reason why. We believe that we should have better treatment in regard to our cattle, and that we should have better treatment in the markets of Great Britain. I do not see why the government cannot accept this resolution. It declares that this House regrets that no conclusion was arrived at on this subject. Surely the ministers, or some of them, regret that no conclusion was arrived at. I must correct my hon. friend from Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) in stating that these gentlemen crossed the water and brought nothing home with them. My hon. friend forgets that two or three of them came home with those titles that they formerly spoke of as tin-pot titles. One thing the conference has accomplished, at all events, is that it has enabled some of these hon. gentlemen to get some of their old tin-pot titles. I trust the ministers will take this into their serious consideration and that if they do not arrive at the conclusion to vote for the resolution upon the present occasion, at an early date they will take such steps as will result in impressing upon the British government that Canadians realize that they have done about as much as they intend to for the old land until the statesmen of England are prepared to treat us better than they treat the Russian, the German, the Hottentot and the citizen of every other nation in the world.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the discussion of this question for a great many years in this House and I am bound to say that this discussion, in so far as it has been taken part in by hon. gentlemen on the government benches to-day, has differed from any that I have ever heard in this House before. In defence of the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher), I must say, in his absence, that he was more frank when this question was discussed in this House last year than hon. gentlemen have been on this occasion. Now, Sir, the people of Canada believe this is a very serious question and one which should be seriously considered by both parties in this country, whether Conservative or Liberal. The hon. Minister of Agriculture, last year, when he was asked to produce the papers in connection with the embargo in the motion presented by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) said that the correspondence was very slight, that there was very little correspondence to produce, but that at a later period he would bring it down. But, what did he say in the meantime ?-that he had been in the old country, that he had discqssed the question with the British Minister of Agriculture, that he had been in Edinburgh, that he had discussed the question with a large number of people living in that locality and that the British Minister of Agriculture did
not dispute the statement of the hon. gentleman when he said that Canadian cattle were not diseased. The answer that Mr. Hanbury gave on that occasion was something like this:
Hon. Mr. Hanbury said that while he was quite ready to admit that Canadian cattle were perfectly healthy. . . . disease might break out among them at any moment and In such a case the reimposition of the old embargo would be a difficult matter as it would cause greater disturbance in the trade and make the condition of affairs worse than if a settled policy were followed.
That was the statement that Mr. Hanbury made on that occasion. What followed ? He said in Edinburgh that:
So long as he remained Minister of Agriculture he would neither make nor advise any change in the law.
The ministers representing the Canadian government in England have been at the conference. The right hon. leader of the government (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has stated that this matter was not of sufficient importance for the conference to deal with. If that is true, if the conference viewed it in that light, surely the ministers from Canada had an opportunity of discussing this question with the British Minister of Agriculture, or with the English government. If the government had made it a point that an important question of this kind should be discussed with the British Minister of Agriculture, or with other gentlemen representing the English government, and then, if they had discovered that the English government were not prepared to amend the law, that they were not prepared to admit Canadian cattle, what would be the use of wasting time discussing the removal of the embargo from Canadian cattle in Great Britain? If that is a settled policy of Great Britain on this question, it is simply a waste of time to discuss it here. Let our ministers be frank with us and say to the House that the British government are not prepared to change the law and that it is useless to look for the removal of the embargo on Canadian cattle. Has Canada anything in her possession that would be of advantage to Great Britain ? Is there anything by which Canada can enter into some arrangement with Great Britain and by which Canadians can have the advantage of sending their cattle to Great Britain ? If this could be done, I think it would be a long step in the right direction, but to pursue the course we are pursuing now is simply a useless waste of time in my judgment, and nothing will be accomplished.

Mr. Speaker, as I come from a part of the country where thousands of dollars are invested in the cattle industry, I thought it would not be out of place to make a few remarks on this question although I cannot hope to add anything of an original character to the debate. We had a resolution during the last

session introduced by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) which was intended, as he stated, to strengthen the hands of the government in the endeavour at the interimperial conference to bring pressure to bear upon the imperial government in order to have this embargo removed, and as far as we can learn fx-om the public press and from the other documents at our disposal nothing transpired at the conference to show that the government took those steps that we Canadians expected they would take as our representatives. They seem to have screened themselves to-day behind the plea: Wait until the papers are brought down and then you will see whether anything in our actions should merit your condemnation or not. There would be no impropriety in the members of the government, who had this conference with Mr. Hanbury, explaining at least the gist of what arguments were bi'ouglxt to bear on him, and then we would be in a better position to know whether to condemn the government or not. Since the resolution was passed in the House last session, Mr. Henderson, of Scotland, the representative of the Canadian Cattle Importation Association, has been in Canada, and he has spoken before our Boai'ds of Trade and other bodies who are interested in having this embargo removed. Mr. Henderson has urged that strong resolutions should be addressed by the Canadian parliament to the imperial parliament, and he has stated his own opinion that it is useless further to approach Mr. Hanbury after the remarks that gentleman has made on the question.
The Prime Minister read to-day from an imperial document, a statement that the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mu-lcck) was delegated by the Canadian government to interview Mr. Hanbury. If there is any member of this government who could fill this mission with least grace it is the Postmaster General, because as the member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has shown he was the member of the Liberal party who from this side of the House condemned the Conservative government for relaxing the quarantine regulations between the United States and Canada which was alleged to be the reason why the embargo was levied in the first place; and he is now a member of a government who did away with the ninety days quarantine thus allowing the free intermixture of the cattle of the United States with the cattle of Canada. Mr. Hanbury now admits that there is no disease among our Canadian cattle, but he says it would not be advisable to remove the embax'go because it would injure the trade in Irish cattle. Evidently he has an eye more to Irish votes than he has to doing justice to Canadian cattle, and in that respect Mr. Hanbury is probably playing the politician rather than the statesman. Mr. Hanbury has ventured the opinion that Canada is not a loser, because we can fatten our cattle and get more per head for them than if the Mr. ROCHE (Marquette).
embargo were, removed, but I take it that our Canadian people are better judges as to whether we are losers or gainers, and if you consult practical cattle exporters such as the hon. member for Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike), Gordon and Ironsides and others, they will tell you that we are lieayy losers by reason of this embargo. At the present time our cattle are admitted only at the port of Glasgow in Scotland, at three or four ports in England, and at no port at all in Ireland. They have to be slaughtered within ten days after landing, and as the hon. member for North Middlesex (Mr. Sherritt) has pointed out, the beef deteriorates on the passage across, and having to be sold merely to local butchers without competition, only the lowest price can be obtained. If other ports were opened and this embax-go removed, not only the local butchers bxxt the bixtchers from all over Great Britain would be present to purchase our cattle and competition being keener the prices would be better. I believe also that no cold storage facilities are px'ovided at the ports of entry, which is a further loss to us. Mr. Henderson who is a practical man has estimated, notwithstanding Mr. Hanbury to the contrary, that there is a loss on our cattle of from $10 to $15 per head because of this embargo. It has been pointed out to-day that one million Canadian cattle have gone to England since the embargo, and at the lowest estimate of $10 per head that means a loss of $10,000,000 to Canada. In his interview with the Winnipeg Board of Trade, Mr. Henderson stated that 8,000,000 consumers in England were in favour of the removal of the embargo and that they were supported in this by a large section of the British press, and by a large number of the members of the House of Commons. I will not say that the abolition of the quarantine between Canada and the United States is a bar to the removal of the embargo on our cattle in England, but if there be a suspicion in the minds of the English people that there is disease amongst United States cattle, our quarantine regulations would have to be more stx-ingent than they are at present in order that the British embargo might be removed. It has been stated by the Prime Minister that .Tolxn Bull never mixes up sentiment with business. I quite agree. The embargo on our cattle is an evidence of it. He has in profound words of wisdom in trade xnatters said :	That business is business, and sentiment is sentiment, and business is no more sentiment than sentiment is business. John Bull looks out for No. 1, and he thinks all the more of any son of his who does the same thing. I do not think we are standing in our own light either commercially or sentimentally when we inform the Bi-itish government that so far as Canada is concex-ned we are granting a preference of 33J per cent on Imports from England, and that she should gi'ant a preference,

or rather do us justice in removing the stigma which is now placed on Canadian cattle by condemning them before the whole world as diseased. We do not ask any preference for our cattle over the cattle of any other country which is free from disease. We are told in England that they cannot remove this embargo from Canadian cattle without removing it from American cattle as well, and we might as well say that Canada should have a fiscal policy universal to the whole world and should not give a preference of 33$ per cent on British goods. In view of the fact that we have already granted Great Britain a preference, it is natural for us to expect that our cattle should be admitted to the British market when they show a clear bill of health. It has) been proven beyond peradventure that there is not any disease among Canadian cattle, and now that Mr. Hanbury has been forced to admit that no disease exists, why should not the embargo be taken off unless it be retained as a system of protection- unless Mr. Hanbury is practising protection while he is preaching free trade exactly as our government is doing in Canada. We are therefore only calling upon the Canadian government to do their duty when we ask them to show stronger reasons why we should not pass this motion condemning them. I think, Sir, that they could without any impropriety tell us what took place between the Postmaster General and Mr. Hanbury, notwithstanding the fact that the papers are not yet on the Table of the House.
Mr. EDWARD HACKETT (West Prince, P.E.I.) This question is of great importance to the farmers of Canada, and as I am a farmer myself, I take a great interest in it. A great deal has been said with regard to the sentiment in Great Britain towards Canada and the loyalty and patriotism of the people of Canada. We are all proud of what Canada has done in connection with the trouble in South Africa ; and after our young men have shed their blood on the veldt of South Africa in upholding the British flag, and after Canada has granted a preference in her markets to the products of Great Britain, the government of Great Britain should at least show a preference to our cattle in their markets over those of foreigners. Instead of that, they have been insisting on protection to the farmers of England against the farmers of Canada, and at the same time, as my hon. friend says, blackening the character of the products of Canada. If we are going to have a united empire all round the globe, then the people of all parts of the empire should be treated in the same way. Some hon. gentleman has stated that Mr. Hanbury wishes to protect the Irish cattle. Sir, the Irish people have done no more for Great Britain than the people of Canada, and there is no more reason why the cattle of
Ireland should be protected than the cattle of Canada. Why is that embargo not removed at this time ? A year ago we were told that we should have a short session because the premier of Canada and the local premiers were going to England to have a great colonial conference for the purpose of advancing the interests of Canada. For that reason we made the session short. The premier has said this evening that the session may be so long a one that the snow may whiten the ground before it comes to an end. If it does, it will be because a large amount of government work was left over from last session to allow these gentlemen to go to England to take part in that conference. What have they accomplished ? Somebody says they were looking after tin-pot titles. I do not know that they have brought many back. The premier of Prince Edward Island went to attend that conference, and it was stated in the government organ of that day that he would come back as Sir Arthur Peters. He did not, however. He came back as plain Mr. Arthur Peters.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

Before recess, Mr. Speaker, I was pointing out the importance of this question. We know in general that stock raising is the principal part of the farming industry, and that in order to effectively promote that industry we should have the right of entry on the English market, the same as British subjects all over the United Kingdom. Since recess there has been placed in my hands the Montreal ' Star ' in which there appears the following dispatch :
London, March 24.
The statement of the Secretary of War, Rt. Hon. St. John Broderick, in the House in reply to Mr. Alfred Davies, shows that the War office still excludes Canadian beef from the army contracts.
That, I consider, a very unfair policy. Why should Canadian beef be excluded ? The people of Canada are just as loyal to the British flag as those of the United Kingdom, and while we are willing to shed our blood for the British flag, the British people should at least give a preference to Canadian beef over beef from the Western States. I would ask that this resolution moved by my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell) should be adopted by the government without division. Our Canadian farmers are the mainstay of the Dominion. They are the men who provide the bread and beef for the people of Canada and who also ship a large surplus to other countries. They therefore should be looked upon as the first people to be protected by the government of this country. I see by the Year-book of

1901 that the value of our exports to Great Britain amounted to $8,000,000. Well, if we were allowed equal privileges with the people of Ireland and Scotland, if our cattle were admitted into the markets of Great Britain without being subjected to this embargo, our exports would amount to $1,000,000 more in the year. That is something worth contending for, and I trust that the government will see the importance of adopting this motion and allow it to be adopted unanimously.
Before recess I said a few words about the trip made to England by our ministers to attend the coronation festivities. Their expenses were paid by the Canadian people and our people were entitled to expect some results. We supposed that when the Prime Minister of Canada and the premier of each of our provinces attended the conference of premiers of the whole empire at London, they would bring back some tangible result. But, Sir, they came back with nothing. The only thing they accomplished was the passing of some resolution with regard to weights and measures, but not one single thing in favour of the Canadian people did they accomplish. There was one result, however, from the trip which was worth noting. During their absence, the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte), who was alive and active to the interests of the Canadian people, was advocating what should be done to promote our wealth and our prosperity, but when these gentlemen returned to Canada the right lion, the First Minister asked the Minister of Public Works to resign. Why did he ask him to resign ? Simply because the ex-minister was advocating the interests of the Canadian people. We are told by the hon. gentleman on the Treasury benches that they cannot reply to the motion of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) because the Minister of Agriculture has gone to Japan. Is that a reason which we ought to accept ? Why should ministers of the Crown, who are paid to reply to questions of this kind, be unable to reply because one of their number happens to be in Japan ? I say that the gentleman who is at the head of so important a department as that of Agriculture should be here to answer the questions put to him by the representatives of the people, and when he is not here he is derelict in his duty. I trust the government will allow the motion of the gentleman for Pictou to pass without a vote because it affects the interests of a large part of the population of Canada. Should this matter come up in the imperial parliament what would they say ? They would say :	You divided on this question in Canada which shows that you have different opinions concerning it. This is not a motion of want of confidence, Mr. Speaker, but a motion in the interests of the Canadian farmer, and I trust the government will take that into consideration and allow it to pass without calling for a vote.
Mr. HACKETT

I see that the right hon. the leader of the government is not here, but in his absence I would make a suggestion to his hon. colleague the Minister of Finance. The opposition desire to get the unanimous opinion of the House on the important matter brought up by my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell). But as the Finance Minister has declared that he will call upon his friends to vote down the motion and as he has promised to have the papers laid on the Table in two'or three days, I would suggest to my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell) that he should withdraw his motion in order that he may have an opportunity, when the papers come down, of renewing it should they not be in accordance with his opinion. We do not want to prejudice the matter at all, it is not a question of private politics, we have no desire to make political capital out of it, our only desire is to have this embargo removed, and therefore with the consent of the government I would suggest that my hon. friend, if the government will consent, should withdraw his motion, reserving the right to renew it on another occasion when the papers are before the House.
The government can have no objection to the hon. gentleman withdrawing his motion.
On the understanding that the hon. gentleman will not be estopped from dealing with the same subject on another occasion.

Whatever is open to the hon. gentleman within the rules of the House, he is free to do. I am not aware of anything which would prevent his bringing the matter up again. But that is a matter that will have to be governed by the rules of the House.

The leader of the House in his place to-day stated that he thought these papers would be laid upon the Table-in the course of this week. In that case, if the government Will-as I have no doubt they will-use diligence in giving us these papers at an early day, as I would much prefer that the resolution would be prepared that would be unanimously supported, I would ask leave with the consent of my seconder that I withdraw my motion.
Amendment withdrawn.
I would like to ask what is the earliest day when we could expect the Redistribution Bill.
The Bill is in a very advanced stage. I would not like to fix a definite date for its introduction, but I can promise that it will be introduced very shortly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext:
Before the motion for Committee of Supply is put,
I would ask the Minister of Justice if it is ; the intention of the government to introduce a general telephone law this session ?

I think that when the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) asked that question before, the leader of the House suggested that there should be a formal notice. The Prime Minister is absent at the moment, but if the hon. gentleman will put a notice on the paper it will be a reminder, and an answer will be given.
I think this is sufficient notice, and the next time the Committee of Supply is moved for I shall press for an answer.
The hon. gentleman cannot get an answer if we have not one ready for him.

Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I would like to call your attention and that of the House to a matter of very great importance to the city of Montreal. I refer to the vacancy in St. James division. We have had the announcement in the speech from the Throne that very important matters in connection with the transportation question and other matters of interest to the city of Montreal are to be brought up this session. I think it extremely desirable that this important division of the city of Montreal should be represented without delay in this House, as its interest in these questions is so great. You, Mr. Speaker, have, no doubt, issued your warrant, and an election can be had there in time enough to have here from St. .Tames division a representative who will be able to sit and deliberate upon these important questions. Besides, the division having been represented as it has been for the past two sessions, and in view of other circumstances to which I need not refer, it is but right and pvoper that an election should be had there without delay and the division represented. I do not think it should be necessary to insist at length upon the urgency of this matter. I live in the division and have a vote there, and I know that the electors of the division are extremely anxious to be represented in the present session. I would ask the government if it is the intention to have an election there without delay.

My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) is, no doubt, aware that there has been a special finding in that case, and a report that there was a general system of bribery in the election. Under these circumstances, the question arises whether the
warrant should be issued direct by the Speaker, or whether it should not be taken cognizance of by the House itself. There are several precedents on the subject, and we must consider them.
speakername: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick).

speechtext: I was not aware that there was such a report.

As my name was brought into the discussion, I may inform the hon. member (Mr. Monk) that I was prevented from issuing my warrant because a report was made that a general system of corruption had prevailed in the election. Section 48, chapter 9, of the Revised Statutes seemed to cover the case and to prevent my issuing my warrant.
Is it the intention of the Minister of Justice to bring it before the attention of the House ?
It is a matter to he considered by the House, not by the Department of Justice.
When will it be brought before the House ?
At the proper time.
I see by a report in the Toronto ' Globe ' that it is likely that the budget speech will be made on Thursday next. Is there any intention on the part of the Finance Minister to-
The report is not correct. An announcement will be made, as usfial, a couple of days in advance.

I do not know that this is the best time for bringing up a matter to which I wish to refer, but I think I shall be in order in doing so. I notice in yesterday's paper a cable despatch, part of which reads as follows :
The Earl of Rosebery will to-morrow move in the House of Lords : ' That this House expresses its approval of the establishment of a council of national defence and earnestly hopes that the first efforts of such a council will be directed to the adjustment of national armaments, to the naval, military and financial conditions of the empire.' Lord Rosebery will then probably make an announcement upon the question of colonial contributions, probably urging that it is necessary for the colonies to send members to the House of Commons, and reform the Lords as the necessary preliminary.
Has the Minister of Finance any information he can give us ns to any correspondence going on between the government here and the colonial office regarding this question ?

I have no information, I am afraid, that I can give my hon. friend. I need hardly remind him that Lord Rosebery is not in the imperial government. He speaks from the opposition side. Whatever views he may have, he would hardly open official correspondence with the government of the Dominion. However, I am hardly in a position to give the hon. gentleman any information upon the subject.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Public works, chargeable to income-public buildings, Nova Scotia-Halifax, new public buildings, $60,000.
Would the hon. Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) have any objection to leaving this item over until my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Borden) returns ?
I have no objection, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) desires it. But I do not think this is a debatable item.
speakername: The MINISTER OP PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. Mr. Sutherland).

speechtext: It is not a new item, but it is to provide for the continuation of the work upon a building begun a year ago.

The building is under contract, and $60,000 is what the architect estimates will be spent ^he comin" year. This is in addition to $50,000 already voted. All particulars and details with regard to the building "Jv<La!ready been given. Besides, if desired, there will be another opportunity to discuss the matter.
I do not think the hon. member for Halifax would wish to have it kept over.

Generally, what is the explanation of the item ?
The MINISTER OP PUBLIC WORKS This is for a public building at Halifax, the contract for which was let on the 30th June last.
What is the building for -a post office ?

Customs house and general offices.
The MINISTER OP PUBLIC WORKS The chief architect of the department has made a careful estimate, and he thinks that $60,000 is all that can be expended on this building.
What is the total amount ?
$250,000 is the amount of the contract. The total amount expended to the 31st of December was $43,874. That Includes the site. Mr. SPROULE.
When does the contract call for the completion of the building ?

On the loth of September, 1904. Of course the balance we are asking for will be for the fittings, &c. The contract is given to the lowest tenderer, M. E. Keefe, of Halifax.
Quarantine station, Lawlor's Island, $1,500.

This is for repairs.
Public buildings, New Brunswick-Ricbibucto, $10,000.

This building is under contract for $9,716. The contract was made on the 15th of November, 1902, and the building is to be completed by January, 1904. The balance is required for heating, boilers, fittings, &c. The total cost is estimated by the architect at $15,000. It is a general public building for post office, custom house, &c.
What was the statement of the Minister of Public Works last year as to the probable cost of this building ?
I have not got that information. I will be pleased to look it up and bring it down. The total cost estimated by the architect, including everything, is $15,000.
There seems to have been a vote of $5,000 last year. What was the promise made to the House as to the probable expenditure ?
I cannot say what statement was made last year. I will make a memorandum and find out, if the hon. gentleman wishes.

Who is the contractor in this case ?
The MINISTER OP PUBLIC WORKS James Reid, Sydney, N.S. He was the lowest tenderer.
Has there been any change in the plans with regard to that building ?

I am informed that no change has been made in the plans and specifications as they were first send out.
St. John, immigration building, $12,000.

This is to provide for the foundation, and to make some alterations required in the St. John immigration building. Representations were made by the city, by the steamship companies and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, that there was not room enough to accommodate immigrants | landing at St. John, and it is necessary to

make these improvements for their accommodation. I may explain that we are putting a third story on the present building, and increasing the fire protection. The third story is estimated to cost $10,000.
What was the total amount expended on those buildings ?
The amount previously expended was $35,517. It is a pretty large building.
Did you expend the money voted last year ?
Yes.
Could the minister give us an idea of the probable number of immigrants that will land there ? I thought they usually came by Halifax.

I have not got a summary of the number that have arrived. But we had communications from the Immigration Department that it was necessary to increase the accommodation for second-class passengers. The Elder-Dempster Steamship Company expect to land at St. John 2,000 immigrants per week for the season of 1903. The Allan Steamship Company, whose boats arrive on the same day as the Elder-Dempster line, also expect to bring large numbers of immigrants.
The present year ends on the 30th of June.
That means for the present season. They were urging that this work should be done early this season. We have also communications from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company urging improvements.

The present building is a great deal too small. A few weeks before I left office, I went down there and saw myself that the size of the building ought to be increased. It was built too small at first.

I am sure that we are obliged to the bon. member for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) for the information he gives us, and which it is almost impossible to get from the Minister of Public Works. It is a good thing that the hon. gentleman is in the House, because otherwise we would be pretty much in the dark as to what is going on in that department.

I do not mean to convey any new information, but as I was Minister of Public Works when that increase was decided upon, I thought it would be no harm for me to tell what has come to my personal knowledge.

That is what I said. We are thankful to the hon. gentleman, and the House is pleased that we have him
here to give us information that we cannot get from other sources.

I have been only a short time in the department, and I am pleased indeed to get any information from the ex-Minister of Public Works, or any other member that is able to give it. I am most anxious to give all the information provided for me by the officials of the department.

The House is well aware that the Minister is new in the position, and he is no doubt doing his best. Are these immigrants expected to remain long at these seaports ? Do they not push right through, and should not facilities be afforded for expediting their departure from the seaports ?

There is a certain delay at these landing ports. I have satisfied myself from the information given to me by the steamship companies and the railway companies, as well as by the immigration agent responsible for the report which he makes to the department, that this increased accommodation is really necessary. I may say to the committee that when we consider the number of people arriving and likely to arrive during the present season we will see that they can hardly be properly accommodated even when the increased provision that we propose is made. There are on the way now on one of the Allan ships 1,800 immigrants who will arrive at St. John, and the Elder Dempster Company inform us that they will be bringing about 2,000 immigrants a week. Therefore, the accommodation which we propose to provide will scarcely provide for the large numbers which are coming, and I am informed that it is really necessary.
I understood from the hon. minister that the total cost of the improvements would be $12,000.
The balance.
Then, the total amount of the improvements will be $22,000, $10,000 last year and $12,000 this year ?

Yes.
St. John Quarantine station-water service, drainage, heating, &c., $8,000.
Would the hon. minister be kind enough to tell us what steps have been taken in reference to this water service ?

This vote of $8,000 is to provide fresh water to the quarantine stations on Partridge Island. It is necessary to carry the water main across the channel from the city to the different quarantine buildings. The estimate has been made by the chief architect
Wliat is the total amount required ?
This work is estimated to cost $24,000. I have all the items here if the hon. gentleman requires them.
It seems an enormous sum for drainage and the connection of the water1. works with these buildings.

Yes, it has been a costly work, but I think the committee will agree with me when I say that it is very necessary that these unfortunate people who are quarantined there, some ill and some not, should be supplied with drinking water.
Is the quarantine station on Partridge Island ?
Yes.
What is the distance over which we have to carry this pipe to connect with the quarantine station ?
The main is 5,400 feet long to be carried from the city across the channel.
I would like to ask the hon. minister whether he will ask for tenders, or whether he intends carrying out the work himself with his own officers ?
I am informed that au arrangement has been made with the city of St. John to do that part within the city and the balance will be done under contract let by tender.
I would like to ask the hon. minister what part he intends doing himself ?
About three-quarters of the expenditure will be for work done by the department under tender and contract.
What kind of work does my hon. friend want to make a contract for-the laying of the pipe across the harbour ?
Yes.

Let me draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Public Works to the enormous expenditure for a purpose of that kind. Twenty-four thousand dollars would furnish a small town in Ontario with a water works system.

Well, I am informed by the deputy minister that every effort has been made to procure water in other ways. Tests were made for artesian wells and it has been found that this is the only system by which they can get a plentiful supply.
Will there be an extra charge for the water in addition to the cost of these works ?
Is the city of St. John paying any part of this expenditure or do we pay it all ?
I do not think there is any reason why the city should be called upon to pay for any part of the work. It is entirely for the benefit of the quarantine station.
We get the water from the city water works ?
Yes.
Is there any understanding as to a permanent arrangement and as to what charge shall be made for water by the city ?
Yes, we will pay $252 per annum.
Is that for a length of time or for one year only ?
It is by the year for the present; there is no fixed time.
Did I understand the hon. Minister of Public Works to say that the installation of a water service and a drainage system at the quarantine station in St. John was going to cost $24,000 ?
Yes. *

I think, under the circumstances, the committee is entitled to some more details. It seems an immense sum to pay to supply the quarantine station with fresh water and a system of drainage. Even $5,000 would do a great deal but $24,000 entitles the committee to some details as to how that sum is going to be expended. We are absolutely in the dark as to the details of the expenditure, and it appears such a large item that I think we ought to go into the details.

Well, I do not know that there is any other information that can) be desired whieh can be given by the department. If my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) wants a detailed statement of every item as estimated by the architect I will be very pleased to bring it down and give it to him. I have not these details here, but in a general way I have given the fullest possible explanation and all the information that is in my possession.

My hon. friend has given no explanation at all. In view of the largeness of the item, $24,000 for providing the quarantine station with fresh water and a system of drainage, I would like to know

how much of this is going to be spent in plumbing, for instance ? If there is to be a pumping station to pump the fresh water how much of this sum goes for that ?
The water will be taken from the city water works, so that there is no pumping station required.
I never heard of such an amount as $24,000 to provide such an establishment as this with water and heating and drainage. What sum is to be applied under each of these heads ?

The building, is already heated, but a pipe 5,400 feet long has been laid from the city of St. John, through the channel to the island, and the excavation is very expensive. A careful estimate of the cost of the work has been made by the chief architect, and he says it cannot be done for less than this sum. Last session $17,000 was voted but that was found insufficient, and it was deemed better to wait until enough money was voted before going on with the work.

I must say that we find very great difficulty here in getting proper details in connection with large items of expenditure. No school board, no municipal council, not to speak of an individual, would say that the amount here asked to vote for this purpose, is at all within a reasonable limit. We had better postpone this vote until we get those details which any ordinary administrative body would be entitled to. I have no desire to delay the business of the House, but I do say that this item should not pass until we get sufficient information.

I agree that the fullest possible detailed information should be given on every vote, but I think the information given with regard to this vote is full and sufficient. It is most inconvenient to allow these items to stand, and I will suggest to the hon. gentleman that if he is not satisfied, then at a later stage I will bring down the detailed statement made by the chief architect, if the hon. gentleman wishes.

I cannot agree to that proposition, because on many occasions we have been told that detailed information would be brought down afterwards, and for one reason or another we have never seen it. Here we are asked to vote $25,000 under the heading of water service, drainage, and heating, for a quarantine station, and I am in the judgment of the House when I say that this appears at first sight to be an exorbitant sum to ask for such a purpose. The minister cannot tell us how much of this money goes for water service, how much for drainage and how much for heating. Surely, with his deputy minister at his elbow, he ought to be able to give in-14
formation on that point. I am again in the judgment of the Committee when I say that we have not had a single satisfactory explanation to enable us to pass this vote.

I also am in the judgment of the Committee when I say that it has never been customary in this House to ask for the number of nails and the number of feet of lumber which enter into the calculation of the architect. I think I have given the fullest possible explanation in a general way, and I have proposed to the hon. gentleman that if he is not satisfied I will bring down the detailed information later. Why, it would take tons of paper if we were to bring down full details in connection with every departmental item, such as this.
What information has been given already ?
Would the hon. gentleman be kind enough to tell me what information he would like ?

I asked the minister to distinguish between the cost of water service, the cost of the drainage, and the cost of the heating, and he was unable to do so. The minister tells us that it is unusual to ask for such information. I have not been in this House so long as he, but my parliamentary experience extends from 1886, and I can say that not only is it usual but that it is the rule to ask and to obtain such detailed information. While the Hon. Mr. Tarte was Minister of Public Works, when these details were asked for they were always given and given cheerfully. That hon. gentleman (Mr. Tarte) knew everything that was connected with his department, and the same rule should be followed now.

The same rule is being followed. I think my hon. friend gave every detail at that time, and I do not think it could be expected that that should be given over and over again, especially when I have promised to bring down full details of the estimate made by the architect for the work.

When I left the department the position was this. The department had tried to dig artesian wells, and a great deal of money had been spent without getting water, although the experts had told us that we could get water easily. Then it was suggested that a system of surface water could be arranged for. I went down during the month of August, and it was not very difficult for me to make up my mind that that suggestion had no sense whatever. The only practicable means of getting water for a quarantine station is to lay a pipe across the bay, a distance of 5,000 or 6,000 feet at least, to connect with the city of St. John water system. It is a very rocky place.

How much would that
cost ?
It would cost $20,000 or $25,000 at least.
Then we are not voting enough.

Of course, I have not the details. I had Mr. Shewen, our chief engineer, make a complete report on the matter. When I left the department that report had not been received. It is very important that we should have water at the quarantine station, and I am very much surprised and sorry that we have not sooner provided the accommodation that we should have there.
One would infer, from the hon. gentleman's remarks, that it was proposed to bury the pipe in the rock. Surely that is not the intention. It might rest on the bottom of the bay.

When my hon. friend who has just spoken rose, I was about to rise for the purpose of making a statement of the facts so far as I know them, and they entirely correspond with the statement made by the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte). The problem of obtaining a water supply for Partridge Island has been a very serious one indeed, and has given to all who have been interested in the matter a great deal of anxiety and concern. I am personally acquainted with the efforts that were made in the direction stated by the ex-Minister of Public Works, which efforts failed. Partridge Island is simply a rock where no water has been found or is likely to be found.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What is the distance from the city.
About a mile across the west channel of the harbour.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
About 5,000 feet.
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS. Tlie water supply is obtained from the western or Carleton side of the harbour, in connection with the public supply, and I do not believe it will be possible to secure such supply in any other way than that now proposed by the Department of Public Works. My hon. friend from Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) spoke as if this were a very large expenditure to be made in an unimportant locality.
No.
He rather spoke of the place as not being of special consequence. Of course, if it were in the city of St. John, my hon. friend would at once admit that aiiy reasonable expenditure for any proper
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: purpose would be justified ; but he spoke of the work on this island as if it were not a matter of great importance. I can assure him that a quarantine station at that point is an absolute necessity. Hundreds and even thousands of people are brought into the harbour of St. John, largely immigrants, for the west, and it is of the most vital consequence to the health of the people of Canada that proper precautions be taken there, and that a thoroughly equipped station be established there. What has been done has not been done without much consideration on tlie part of all who were interested in the matter. I think that the sum named in this estimate is a very moderate and reasonable sum. if it is found to be sufficient to cover the actual outlay. I do not wish to speak on that point, however, because I have no special knowledge to qualify me to do so ; but T a in sure that my hon. friends who criticised this item rather severely-
No, no.

Well, I a pi glad to hear that they did not, because I think it will be found, on a searching investigation, that there is no vote asked for in these estimates which is more justifiable or necessary than the one now under discussion.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals has spent some time in eloquently answering a charge which was not made. No one questioned the probable necessity or utility of this work; there was no criticism, so far as I know, on that point at all. The point of criticism, as the hon. minister well knows, was that the hon. Minister of Public Works was unable to give any information. My hon. friend from Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) stated specifically the items on which he asked for information, namely, the water service, the drainage service and the heating, and I am sure that my hon. friend will agree that the committee should be put in possession of this information. The hon. Minister of Public Works is pleased to say that he will bring down the information after we have passed the item, and if it is not found to be satisfactory he will consent to a rehearing of the case. Surely my hon. friend would not propose a course of that kind in this House. Where would it end ? He knows that we could not do that kind of thing. He knows that without the consent of the House the case could not be heard again. If the hon. gentleman would give us the information, we would be under no necessity of putting these questions to him. I am going to take the liberty of asking again what is the cost of the heating and the nature of the heating, what is the cost of the drainage service and the character of that drainage, what is the cost of the water service, whether there is a contract with the city of St. John and what is the Dature of that con-

tract, liow long is that contract to continue and what sum is to be paid. Those are very reasonable questions and it is no severe criticism to ask the Minister of Public Works for the information.

I thought that I had answered the most important of the questions the hon. gentleman put, but I find that the department are a little short in some of the details we should have with regard to this expenditure. The item is somewhat misleading. This $12,000, I understand, was for the purpose of putting in a water pipe under an arrangement with the city. The pipe has to be extended down to tide water, and we agreed to pay two-thirds of the cost on the report of the engineer, our share being some $4,000 out of $6,000. I would prefer having the item stand until I can have an opportunity of sending to the department for further details.

Before the hon. minister leaves St. John harbour, I would take the liberty of drawing his attention to another point. I understand that the Public Works Department is charged with the care of the historical landmarks of the country. At the mouth of the River St. John is old Fort Latour, built in the very early days of the settlement of North America by the Huguenots, and one of the most interesting landmarks of the country. I would suggest to the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Railways that an appropriation should be made to keep that old fort in a state of preservation. I am sure that the descendants of the old Huguenots, who were the first French colonists in that portion of British North America, will be greatly pleased if the government should do so.

To how much water is the quarantine station entitled for this $200 a year ? Is any arrangement made for the use of this water for protection against fire ? If the city have the right to sell this water at a high price, we should not pay such a large share of the cost of laying down the main. The city is getting a good return for its disbursements and we ought to know what we are getting for ours.

I find that I have not the report from the engineer in charge at St. John, and would ask that the item be allowed to stand.
Item allowed to stand.
Dominion buildings, 13,000.
Was that expended last year ?
That is the same vote asked for a number of years.

That is not sufficient explanation. We are entitled to know every year how the money is to be expended. If we put a new furnace last year in a building, we require to know what we are going to do to that building this year and should have a statement showing how that $12,000 are to be expended.

There is a general vote for repairs to public buildings throughout the province. It would be quite impossible to tell just what repairs would be required for the coming year, for unforeseen conditions will arise. We can only account for the money that was voted in previous years, and my hon. friend knows that that is given in the fullest detail in the Auditor General's Report. I can give the hon. gentleman the details of expenditure for the past year.
I do not require that, so far as I am concerned. But I would like to know how this sum of $12,000 is divided.

I quite agree with the hon. gentleman that, if the annual vote were too large or too small, the minister would have to explain why he asked for so much, or would be obliged to ask for an increase. For the past year, for instance, I have a list here of repairs running from 75 cents to $800, and applying to twenty or thirty public buildings throughout the province, and amounting in all to about $7,000. That left a balance of $5,000 unexpended. The deputy minister informs me that this $12,000 is about the usual amount required from year to year for the maintenance of the different buildings throughout the province.
Do these repairs cover furniture ?

No, we have a separate vote for that. This is only for repairs to the buildings themselves.
Public Works-chargeable to income, public buildings, Quebec-Dominion public buildings- renewals, improvements, repairs, &c., $12,000.
Would the hon. minister tell ns how this is divided ?
It is a pretty long list, but I will give my hon. friend the expenditure so far this year, which amounts to $11,988.

What I wished to know is not how this money was expended last year, but how this estimate is made up-what amount is allotted to the different parts of the province. A board of school commissioners, for instance, will provide a certain
*

amount for repairs at each school. What I want to know, in two words is what is the hon. minister's basis of calculation in making up his estimate.

The estimates are not made up in the way suggested by the hon. gentleman. They are made up on the basis of a number of years' experience. Showing what is likely to be required for the repairs of the public buildings in the province. Owing to special causes, much more may be required in one place than in another. For instance, we spent in the Aylmer public building this year, $166 ; in Hochelaga, $404 and in Drum-mondville, only $8. The committee will easily see that the necessity for repairs arises from causes which cannot be foreseen. The method of the department in the past has been to get the vote which experience has shown to be necessary.

If that is the system adopted, I believe this is the only administration throughout the country, the only public body where such a system is followed. The hon. gentleman thinks what has been spent in the past is a guide for what he shall ask in the future. He tells us we have spent $166 on the Aylmer building. I suppose he counts on the same amount next year. Does the hon. minister mean to say that, before this item is made up those in charge of the different buildings are not required to send in an estimate of the repairs that will be necessary ? I venture to say there is not a board of school commissioners, nor municipal body throughout the country where such a plan is not adopted.
The hon. gentleman says he has had great experience in school and municipal bodies-
I did not say that, but I was speaking of what everybody knows to be their method.

Well, I have had experience in both, and I take issue with the hon. gentleman. Every one can understand that there are certain unforeseen contingencies which involve expense and which must be provided for. In the case of the department, if any repairs are required at the first of the fiscal year, no douht, reports will have reached the department from the officers in charge of the different buildings. But, suppose a roof leaks, or a pipe bursts, or a door breaks, we cannot know of these things in advance of preparing the estimates. The estimate is made up, I think, in the only business way for places of this kind. We do not expend the money unless it is required. In some cases balances are left over, while, in other cases there is an over expenditure which must be justified and a vote given to cover the amount. .

I entirely disagree with the statement of the hon. minister as to the mode usually adopted by public bodies. Of course, there must be a certain amount provided to cover unforeseen contingencies. But, that we are to be guided entirely by the past, is certainly not a correct system. As has been said, it surely would be expected that the department would ascertain from the parties in charge of the respective buildings what sum each of them would require. A very strange condition of things otherwise would arise. The government is not entitled, as I understand it, to expend the public money unless it is voted by parliament. Unless the information is collected on which to base a careful estimate, we are not in a position to take a fair, business view of what is required within the time the estimates cover.
It may arise that the estimate may be too large, it may just as well arise that it may be too small. Suppose that some of these buildings require extensive repairs, more than have been required for several years, that a large building in some part of the province of Quebec requires reroofing, involving an expenditure of several thousand dollars of this appropriation. Is it a business principle that the department is to close its eyes to this necessary information, and come down here without the first glimmering of knowledge as to what is required in that behalf ? It may well happen that a building which has been used as a public building of the Dominion may be abandoned, or that the repairs have been so extensive that no others may be needed upon it for a long time. I submit that what we are entitled to from year to year is an investigation by the department, and that the result should be placed before us, some general information as to the condition of public buildings and the amount necessary for their repair, judged by their condition at the present time. In addition to that, I admit that provision should be made for contingencies that are unforeseen. We should not discard the past altogether, and judging by the past we can form some opinion of what may be required from year to year. Until we have such an investigation from year to year, and the result laid before parliament, the department is not doing its duty by this Committee or by the people whom we represent.

The hon. gentleman is mistaken. There is another item where provision is made for repairs. This is simply an item for unforeseen expensesi in the various buildings, of which there are 37 or 40 in the province of Quebec. The hon. gentleman will see that it is not a very large amount, considering the value of the property, and the number of buildings for which this general vote is asked to provide for contingencies, In cases where we know that considerable

repairs are required, we ask for another vote and the department give the details for which it is required. Cases do arise, as the hon. gentleman says, every year where unusual damage is done by some heavy storm, for instance, and where the department) has to expend more money than has been voted. In such case we account to parliament for the extra expenditure when the House meets again.

Probably I did not make myself clear to the hon. gentleman, but the item itself is clear. It comes exactly within the lines upon which I addressed myself to the committee. * Dominion public buildings, renewals, improvements, repairs, etc.' I submit that the Minister of Public Works has not explained away the difficulties that arise in the statement lie made that he judged of the necessity of $12,000 by the fact that for several years we have had $12,000 expended.
Grosse Isle-Quarantine station, $12,000.

I will give the details as furnished by the department in regard to this work. It is carried on in accordance with the estimate submitted by the Department of Agriculture. Disinfector for hospital, $2,000; building for bathrooms, $1,800; building for office of surgeon and vaccinating rooms, with four rooms upstairs for non-contagious cases, $2,000; fixing eighteen doors, $18; wire work over baths, $50; bath pipes, $30; smallpox hospital, $40; ventilation, $75; drain to the hospital for water supply, $300; repairs to disinfecting building, $387; repairs to police headquarters, $872; official quarters, $2,000; hydrants, $180; whitewashing, $800; walks, $795 ; incidentals, $353. As the Committee knows, a very large expenditure has been made during the past year at this station. I am informed by the deputy minister that this sum is expected to complete these improvements that are being made in the quarantine station.

If I remember correctly,
it is only a few years ago that we made a similar apparatus for disinfecting.
That was for a general building, this is for the hospital.
Could the minister tell us how much has been expended up to the present time ?
I am sorry to say the department nas not furnished me in this memorandum the total amount expended at, this station.

I have a distinct recollection that for a good many years past we have been spending heavily at Grosse Isle quarantine station, which suggests that the work could not have been mapped cut along intelligent lines at first, otherwise we
would not require to make these improvements from year to year. We were assured a few years ago that the heavy expenditure then required was intended to complete the building. Every year we have the same answer : This is to complete. But we have no guarantee this will complete. Last year we were asked for $10,000, and this year for $12,000. If I remember right, we needed more than that the year before. However, it appears to be going on and I have listened to items being read out which seem to be very much as they were before even to the laying down of the walk. Here is nearly $2,000 for the official quarters. These quarters must be lavishly furnished and very extensive when $2,000 are required to furnish new quarters there after we have been called upon to make these improvements. I think there is either a reckless expenditure or there is something unbusinesslike in the way the money is spent, because we ought to reach a finality some time and we ought to know what this station will cost.

The $2,000 is for a new building. The only information which I can give to the Committee is that this station was established about 1845. The deputy minister informs me that it had gone very much to wreck and that in 1892 the rehabilitation of the whole establishment was commenced. We have spent, up to the present time, about $200,000. I quite agree with my hon. friend that in laying out a work like this if a full, detailed statement had been given and the expenses known it probably would have been better. The deputy minister informs me that this about completes the work as a quarantine station.
Who is in charge of the quarantine station now ?
Of course, that is in the Agriculture department. Dr. Martineau is at the head of the station locally.
Dr. Montizambert is at the head of the service.
Yes.
The statement is made by the hon. minister that this about completes the work. What other work is there in contemplation that will be done and what is the probable cost of completing It ?

Mr. Chairman, this estimate is based on a request made by the Department of Agriculture. We do not expect any further requests for improvements to be undertaken there. If any are received, they will, of course, be closely scrutinized. In connection with a large station like this there would be from time to time some expenditure required, but I trust that for the present there will

be no further improvements of a permanent or substantial character. I visited the station myself last fall and I must say that very great improvements have been made of a very permanent kind and I should think-I can only give the information furnished me by the department-that we should expect no further requests for a large expenditure at this station for some time to come.

Did I understand the hon. gentleman to say that the $12,000 voted last year had been all expended ?
rl'hc MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. Yes.
L'Assomption-public buildings, $10,000.

I see that last year $5,000 was spent and that this year $10,000 is to be expended. Would the hon. minister tell us what the population of L'Assomption is ? The item says ' public building ' but it must be for buildings, because, surely, there would not be an expenditure of $10,000 on one building in a place like this.
I regret I could not hear all the hon. gentleman said, but I understand he asked the population ?
Yes, for the population of L'Assomption.
In the town of L'Assomption there is a population of 1,665 and in the adjoining parish there is a population of 1,275.
What kind of buildings are those that are being put up ?
The building is to be a two and a half storey brick with stone dressings-I suppose the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock) wants to know what the building is for ?
Yes, what is the purpose of it ?
It is a general public building for the post office, &c.
A town hall, or fire stationV Surely, it is not for the collection of customs dues in L'Assomption 7
Sometimes large customs dues are received in small places. I think, however, this is mostly to be used for a post office.

In a town of 1,600 inhabitants, does it not strike you, Mr. Minister, that $15,000 in two years is a very large sum to spend ? I think there must be some mistake. Are they county buildings ? Is it the county of L'Assomption that this building is to be erected for or is it a village building ?

Their municipal constitution down there is Hod. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
different from ours in Ontario. It is more for the town and the parish surrounding it that this post office is furnished.

Does the Dominion of Canada, because there is a difference in the municipal organization, supply municipal buildings in Quebec ? Are the provinces of Ontario and Quebec to supply the wealthy province of Quebec with municipal buildings ? I think there must be some mistake ?

I did not say a municipal building, I said a post office. I do not think my hon. friend (Mr. Brock) is right in insinuating that the province of Quebec has public buildings in small places any more than the province of Ontario has. If there is any rule it has, perhaps, sometimes been violated ; perhaps, occasionally, for some reason or other, we have built public buildings in places where the population and revenue were rather small. The Committee must try and stick to the rule that the revenue and population should be taken into consideration in erecting public buildings. This rule has not been violated any more in Quebec than it has in other provinces.
I would like to ask the hon. minister if a contract for this building has been let, what is the amount of the contract, and what the purpose of the building is.
The contract has been let and it is for a post office.
What is the amount of the contract ?

I would like to ask the hon. minister what the revenue of the post office is at L'Assomption. My reason for asking is that I see an item following, No. 110. public building at the village of Alexandria, $17,000. I suppose that also is for a post office. I would like to get an idea whether it is the policy of the government to erect $17,000 post offices in villages throughout the different provinces. We have one in L'Assomption costing $15,000. and one in Alexandria costing $17,000, and I would like to know what the rule is in regard to post offices in villages of that size ? It seems to me that the revenue must be very small in a village the size of L'Assomption or Alexandria. While I am asking the question I would like to ask also whether these buildings are to be used for any other purposes than that of the post office.

It would be used for all Dominion purposes : customs, inland revenue or any Dominion service. The general policy of the government has not been changed in this respect from the past. It seems to have been the will of the majority of the House

that at least in the chief town of a county there should be a public building erected. Parliament perhaps had not as due regard to revenue as it might have had. In this case the revenue is $942.

The government has certainly not much regard for the revenue received from a town in which they erect a public building. This building will cost more than $10,000, and the population of L'Assomption is 1,605 people. Now, if the government is going to put up a public building in every town of that size which will cost $10,000, where are they going to end ? In my own village we have a court house, a recording office, and a public building, and it is better entitled to a Dominion post office building than is L'Assomption. The government is very extravagant and if they keep on at this rate it must end in failure. I cannot conceive of any other town in the province of Quebec where this expenditure would be so wasted as in the town of L'Assomption.

If that riding estimates that the real reason for returning a representative is whether or not there should be a little public money spent in it, I am quite willing that should be taken as a gauge of the intelligence of the people. It is not only the initial cost of a building that has to be considered. There must be a caretaker, at a salary of $400; there must be fuel at a cost of $200 or $300 more, and so throughout the ridings that return Liberal supporters this expenditure will go on. If towns like Owen Sound and other important centres have the hardihood to oppose the government then they can rest assured that Mr. Justice Lount's principle of warm justice and cold justice will be their reward. It is not the Minister of Public Works alone who is responsible. The whole government pass these estimates, and the whole government is to blame. I remember on one occasion during a session of the late parliament, a grant was made in the riding of East Peterborough to build a dock on a creek, and the hon. member for that riding, who was a government supporter,

defended it on the ground that there had not been any money spent in that riding before. Perhaps these grants may have that same sort of argument to back them up, and nothing else.
Levis public building, $5,000.
What is this sum for ?
This is towards putting up a public building in the town of Levis.
Has the site been acquired?

No. The department has been negotiating with the Department of Railways in the hope that that department may be able to provide a site on land owned by the Dominion. Levis is a growing place and is entitled to a building.

My hon. friend knows that the town of Ldvis is almost all situated on the hill, and if the jjost office is located on a portion of the land belonging to the Railway Department, the people will have to come down from the top of the hill to visit the post office. There must be something wrong here. [DOT]

My hon. friend ought to be more frank and explain the matter fully. He knows that those who have business in LSvis come down by the roads leading to the ferry, and therefore the most convenient place for a public building would be in the neighbourhood of the Intercolonial station. The board of trade of the town of Levis made representations to that effect.

I take issue with my hon. friend, and I would like to see the petitions of the board of trade which represented that the public building of the town of Levis should be situated at the bottom of the hill. My hon. friend and all others who are familiar with the town of Levis know that it extends from the brow of the hill very far back, that a large portion of the population live on the brow of the hill, and that only a few stores are below the hill near the Intercolonial station. If my hon. friends says there was a representation from the board of trade of the town of Levis in favour of such a site, they are in a better position to know than I am; but I would like to see that representation. The public buildings of the town of Levis, as my hon. friend knows, are on the hill. The town hall is on the hill, and if it is convenient to have the town hall there, it would be convenient to have the post office there also.
Mi-. TALBOT. I would ask tile hon. member for Montmorency to be kind enough to tell the House where the market of the town of Levis is-on the top of the hill or below it ?
There are two markets, one below, a very small one, and the larger one on the brow of the hill, near the church.

A deputation from the board of trade of the town of Ldvis, in addition to their written request, visited me at my office in Ottawa a short time ago and urged the selection of this site as in their opinion most convenient for the town. There were present Mr. Carrier, the president of the board of trade, and four or five others. That is the reason of the delay.	-
My hon. friend probably knows that Mr. Carrier's store is at the bottom of the hill, and that is the reason he wanted the post office there.
I happened to be present at the time, and this Mr. Carrier is not the merchant at all, but is connected with Carrier, Lane & Co., and a supporter of the hon. gentleman opposite.
His factory is down there also.
His factory is there, but when he visited the government, he came to make representations on behalf of the people of Ldvis.
If my hon. friend says there is a petition from the board of trade, I would be pleased to see it.
I shall be pleased to have a copy of it sent to the hon. gentleman.

I do not doubt what the hon. Minister of Public Works and the hon. Minister of Justice says; yet it does not look reasonable. They have a post office in Levis close to the station. Then they have one on the top of the hill, on the main road leading south. Are the people of Levis going to close their post office on the top of the hill and go down to the bottom of the hill to get their mail ? It does not look reasonable at all. In the town of Levis there are four post offices. There is a post office half a mile from the station, near Mr. Couture's store, and do you mean to say that he and others have signed a petition to have that post office closed and a general post office placed at the bottom of the hill ? I have no doubt that some people want a good post office near the station, but the rest of the people know nothing at all about it. I know a good deal about that town, and I would like to see some of the people send another petition here. If the people of Levis find out that a petition has been sent here, asking for a post office at the foot of the hill, you will have another to the contrary pretty soon.
