I understood the hon. minister to say that the proposal is to get a site on some land belonging to the Inter-

colonial Railway. That being a government railway, I apprehend that there is not much difficulty in ascertaining quickly whether it will be proper for the Railway Department to part with that land or not. This I find is a revote; the money was appropriated last year. If the ministers are in harmony-of course, we sometimes think they are at loggerheads, and one will not speak to another-how is it that it has not been ascertained up to the present time definitely, whether or not that site is available ? The minister ought to able to tell us what is the difficulty or where the hitch is; so that if we are not going to have that site, we may get another.

I will be pleased again to explain to the hon. gentleman. I was asked how this matter stood. The board of trade of Levis visited Ottawa and made representations to us that this site would be suitable. It turned out that it was on property belonging to the Department of Railways and Canals. We have referred to the chief engineer of railways to know whether or not we can get the land. If we can, it will save considerable expense in the way of securing a site which will be satisfactory to the people.
I understand that instead of the Intercolonial Railway being in a position to dispose of any land, they are anxious to extend their territory.
They do require more land, but it is represented that at this particular place they could spare the small amount that we require.
When did the Public Works Department apply to the Railway Department to see if they could get this land ?

Three weeks ago, when the deputation came up from the town of L6vis.
Montreal examining warehouse-additions and alterations, including fittings, furnishings, &c., $15,000.
I see that we spent $15,000 last year on this same building, and this will make $30,000. How did we spend the $15,000 last year, and what is intended to be done with the $15,000 this year ?

Last year we put an additional storey on the annex. The masonry and brickwork cost $5,050; carpentering work, $3,167; plumbing, $400; heating apparatus, $3,800; concreting roof, $1,200; plastering repairs, $525; tile floor. $700.
Then you have spent $15,000 adding a story. What is this further expenditure for ?
There is besides all the remodelling and furnishings inside.

Two years ago you spent $10,000 painting, kalsomiuing and whitewashing and repainting the third story of the customs warehouse. The following year you added another story. You spent nearly $10,000 finishing the inside and then spent $15,000 the following year adding one more . story. Why are you now spending another $15,000 ?
Two thousand dollars are due on the contract for the furnishing and fittings. The passenger elevator will cost $4,000; lighting fixtures, $3,000, and incidentals. $1,000. This will complete.
Is all this work done by contract ? I notice that always the same contractors get the work.
Every item appears to have been by contract.
Were public tenders asked for ?
They were not advertised for but a number of contractors were asked to tender.

It is a great pity that in Montreal, where we require so much for other improvements, we should spend in three years $40,000 on repairs that, as far as I can judge from the Auditor General's Report and the minister's explanation, appear to have been made wrong side up. We began in 1901-2 completely repairing the customs warehouse, painting, finishing, kal-somining and whitewashing the interior of the building. The following year we tore one-half of the building down in order to put up another story. This year we are going to destroy partly the work we did last year. But what I want particularly to draw attention to is this : This work is done without carrying out the principle of advertising for tenders through the press, and it is always the same men who get the work. Before we vote the $15,000 for next year, we should have the hon. gentleman's assurance that tenders will be called for through the newspapers published in Montreal.

In small appropriations such as this, the advertising would take up the greater part of it. Divide up this into different items and advertise them in the different newspapers for tenders, and you will find that the cost of advertising would take up a considerable expenditure of the appropriation. We ask for tenders from those who are in the trade, and we get all the tenders we would by public advertising and at much less cost.

It is contrary to law that you should undertake a work of $15,000 without advertising for tenders. In the next place, the reason given by the hon. gentleman is surely not serious. All the minister has to do, in order to give the public a chance to compete, is to advertise three or four times in the pap^js published in Montreal, stating where the specifications can be examined. If he does this he will realize an immense saving. We have expended $40,000 in the examining warehouse in Montreal, and I am sure the work could be done for half the price. For my part I would ask the minister to give his pledge before we vote this $15,000 that tenders will be .advertised for in the papers.
I have been looking over the items and I see that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) is right. I shall be prepared to advertise the work for which this $15,000 is voted.

I think this question of advertising or sending out circulars should be discussed in the House. It appears, from the Auditor General's report that the matter has been under discussion during the past year. The Auditor General has called attention to it and has taken the advice of independent counsel as to how far the government has the right to go. I understand the conclusion arrived at to be that where there are only half a dozen people in a particular trade in the Dominion, as, for instance, builders of railway cars or locomotives, it may be proper for the government to send circulars to these people asking for tenders. There is no object in spending hundreds of dollars in advertising where a few circulars will answer the purpose. But, that where there is a general trade, as, for instance, the building trade, the government has no right under the statute-it would be unlawful-to let contracts without advertising in the press. It seems to me absurd for the minister to say in the case of an item of $15,000 that it will cost more than the item to advertise. It ought to cost but a very little sum. If the advertisements were put in the papers of the city of Montreal, I am sure there would be many builders competing for the contract. I only rise to call attention to the facts, because it seems to be the general practice of the government to do as was done in this case.

I undertake to say that that has not been the general practice since I became the head of the department. In practically every case, even the cases involving small amounts, I have advertised in the papers. But there are special cases to be considered. It is very easy for the hon. gentleman to talk, but one of the items in this case, for instance is an elevator. I believe there are only two elevator manufacturers in the Do-Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
minion, both in Toronto. There may be one in Hamilton, though I am not sure.
There are two in Montreal.

Well, even so-we have a list of the people in the business and would send these specifications and ask for tenders. Could we do any better if we advertised ? If we put the advertisement in one paper, at once there would be a howl that it did not go into all. I have carried out the rule of advertising for tenders to the fullest extent, and I intend to do so, unless there is some change in the Act. But I think the department should have more latitude in these small matters, because of the delay and expense and because the public are not so well served as if we were to apply to the reputable people in the trade for tenders.

The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) takes the exception I put to be the rule in his department. If you want an elevator it may be proper to send out a circular to the few manufacturers in that line.
This $15,000, as I explained, is made up of small items like that. We have to advertise each separately.
Of course, every extension of a building involves a number of small items. '

Where there is a large quantity of repairs, as in the present instance, they might be given to one contractor. Or repairs generally might be advertised under specifications which show the details. I believe we spend too much money in advertising for government work. If the law was that repairs, and even more extensive works to be done by the government, should be advertised in such jfiaces as the post offices all over the country, people who wish to tender would go there to look for such advertisements and there would be an immense saving. Of course, that is a matter of administration. But where we see the government spending $40,000 to repair the examining warehouse in Montreal, and when we know what a miserable post office we have, one quite inadequate to meet the requirements of the city, we begin to look with a little caution and to wish that greater care should be taken in the expenditure of public money.	.
Montreal public buildings-improvements, alterations, repairs, &c., $8,000.

I would ask the minister if he has given consideration to this city of Montreal post office. I have called attention repeatedly in this House to the condition of this building. We are erecting public buildings in very insignificant places all over the Dominion, and yet, in the city of

Montreal we have a post office which is absolutely inadequate to the wants of the city. It is a great deal too small and quite insufficient in many ways. I believe the government has had under consideration for several years a scheme by which additional accommodation might be given in the Montreal post office. The hon. minister, no doubt, is aware that the government pays a very large amount of rent in Montreal. I do not know7 the amount, but 1 feel satisfied that it is more than sufficient, if it were capitalized, to give us in Montreal a large post office, where all those government offices now occupying rented premises, could be installed, and where the ministers themselves, when they come to Montreal, would have suitable rooms for the transaction of public business. I do not know if the present minister has given his attention to that subject, but I think some arrangement might be arrived at by which, by spending even less money than is actually spent, we could have a suitable public building in Montreal for the post office and other public buildings as well..

The matter has received some attention since I have been at the head of the department. The Post Office Department have recommended a new system in dealing with the mails in large cities, where they think the service can be more efficiently carried out by the establishment of branch offices. They think that especially in large manufacturing centres it would be better to take the mails from the station, as they do now at Toronto and Montreal, directly to the branch offices. In the city of Montreal it is intended to have a public building at some distance from the present office, which will relieve the congestion in the head office.

Regarding public buildings in large cities, I wish to direct the attention of the Committee to the fact that great progress is being macTe in architecture, and commercial and business reasons now decide the style of architecture rather than outside appearance. Architects will now give you a building that is expressly adapted for the business that you have in view, and I hope that hereafter the department will devote their whole energy, especially in the large cities, in adapting their public buildings to the business they are destined to serve. In Toronto we have a custom house which is a very florid piece of architecture, but is deficient in light. The public have to go up a large staircase in order to do business, there are no elevators, no telephones or anything of that kind. I hope the department will follow the example of the corresponding department in the United States and make their public buildings suited to the purposes, with all modern conveniences, and especially with an abundance of light. These improved
buildings are now being erected in all advanced countries. They have got rid of this idea of monuments, and florid architecture, and sculpture, and are putting up purely business buildings where utility is the chief end in view.
Can the minister state about what amount the government pays in rents in the city of Montreal ?

The Public Works Department are not paying rents for all the departments, so we cannot give the information at the present time. But it is an important subject and I am going to have the amounts made up in Montreal and some other cities, and will give them to the Committee.

Since the attention of the minister has been drawn to the post offices in Montreal and Toronto, I would like to join the chorus of hon. gentlemen opposite and direct the attention of the minister to the post office in the city of Ottawa. This capital city is growing rapidly, proportionately more so perhaps than any city in Canada. The post office was built many years ago, and for a long time it has contained in addition offices for the customs, the inland revenue and the Ottawa Improvement works. Business is certainly in a very congested state in the Ottawa post office, and when the minister is looking into this question I hope he will not forget the capital. Of all the cities I am acquainted with, Ottawa has the greatest need of additional accommodation.

Since attention is being drawn to public buildings in the large cities, I wish to call the attention of the minister to the fact that probably the most urgent case in the Dominion is the post office building in the city of Winnipeg at the present time. This may not be the proper time to speak of that subject on the estimate that is before us, but I would urge the minister to give his attention to Winnipeg, and hope that he will be prepared when the estimates for Manitoba are reached to announce his intentions of providing buildings adequate to the demands of the public services in Winnipeg.

I fully recognize the importance of this question. As the country becomes more prosperous no doubt additional facilities will have to be provided in all the large commercial centres. In regard to Winnipeg, I have had a careful report prepared and will have to ask the House for money to enlarge the building there. The situation in Montreal depends, as I have explained, somewhat on the policy of other departments. I believe it is the intention to build branch offices so as to relieve to some extent the central office. The same remark may be applied to Ottawa. I endorse every-

thing that has been said by the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) with regard to architecture. I think if he will look at station ' O ' built by the chief architect of the department, he will admit that it is a very decided improvement, and will give better satisfaction to the public than a more expensive building. There is no doubt that as regards the large commercial centres the question of increased accommodation will have to be met, and at a later stage I will have to submit some particulars to the House, and perhaps ask for a vote of money for this purpose.

So far as I can gather, this new system of distributing the work of the post office and centreing it around the railway stations instead of taking it all to one building, is in the right direction. It will facilitate the handling of the mails and correspondence and, considered in its purely business aspect, the system cannot be expanded too soon. I am glad to hear the minister say that hereafter he will have the commercial and business aspect more in view in erecting or enlarging public buildings.

I would like to ask the Minister of Public Works if I heard him correctly when he put the question whether there were elevator works at Hamilton. I desire to tell him that the largest elevator works in Canada are established at Hamilton.

I would like to ask the hon. minister for some explanation in regard to the public building in St. Hyacinthe. There was $12,000 spent last year, cr rather $12,000 voted last year and $12,000 is asked for this year. I would like to ask the hon. minister if the $12,000 voted last year was expended or is this a revote ? What are these additions which are to be made to the public building at St. Hyacinthe ?
This is a revote.
It does not say so.
No, it is not a revote.

It should state so. The deputy minister informs me that this sum was voted last year and that none of it was spent, and that this is a revote of the same amount to be expended upon addition to the building there to provide for the excise.
What is the public building for in St. Hyacinthe ? I suppose there is a post office ?

There was a building erected in St. Hyacinthe, if I remember well, about 15 years ago, which has been used for the post office and customs house. About three years ago the division of St. Hyacinthe was enlarged. The excise service is in the same building and there are two or three rooms occupied by the gas and electric inspection service. The building is not sufficient to accommodate all the services. The revenue has increased; it has doubled, or trebled, and a new building is going to be erected next to the present post office.
That is a very satisfactory explanation, but what I would like to know is why] it was that the work was not begun last year. Can the hon. gentleman give a reason for that ?
There was delay in procuring the site as there was some difficulty in the Department of Justice about the title. The matter was just settled two weeks ago.
From whom was the property purchased ?

The first intention was to make an addition to the old building, but as the site was not found convenient the Department of Public Works thought it proper to buy another piece of land. The property was owned by Jule Laframboise, or rather by his wife, formerly Miss Buckley.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Carried.
Has the item been amended ?
There is no amendment necessary.

I submit there would require to be an amendment. The item appears as if $12,000 had been voted last year and that $12,000 is being voted again for the year 1903-4. If it is a revote it should appear in the first column and the item would require to be amended so that it will appear that we are only revoting that amount and not adding $12,000 to the vote of last year.

I was perfectly correct in stating the amount voted last year, but I am mistaken in saying that this is a revote of the same amount. Four thousand dollars has been paid for the site and the chief architect says that the cost of the building will be about $15,000 or $16,000. This would leave the balance of the $12,000 after paying for the site and $12,000 additional.
Do I understand that we are to pay $12,000 in all or $24,000 in all for this building ?
Will that finish the work ?

That will complete the work.
Thetford Mines-public building, $8,000.
May I ask the hon. minister what kind of a public building he is putting up at Thetford Mines ?
The total cost is estimated by the chief architect to be about $10,000.
May I ask what kind of a public building the government is erecting at Thetford Mines ? Is this a post office, custom house, or excise office or is it a mint ?
It is used for a post office and custom house.

I want to call your attention to the fact that the population of Thetford Mines, according to the last census, is 1,605. Yet, you are spending $8,000 for a public building in that locality. I know that there is Thetford North and Thetford South but the population of Thetford South is only 600. Thetford Mines is in Thetford North and the population is only 1,600. In a place of this importance are we going to erect a public building which will cost $12,000 1 I cannot see what you are going to put in the post office or the custom house.
I am pleased to say that the revenue warrants this very much more than some that have been voted. The postal revenue is $2,405, and the customs duties are $3,544, so that the revenue is very good.
I would like to ask the hon. minister whether a site has been acquired ?	.
Yes, the deputy informs me that a site has been procured.
How much has been paid ?
From whom was the site acquired ? Was it given by the village, or the town, or bought outright by the government ?
The site was purchased from King Bros, of Quebec for $1,900.
How much land ?
50 x 100 feet.
The hon. minister gave as a reason for the expenditure in Thetford Mines that there was an income of $2,405 from the post office.
And a customs revenue of $3,544.
And you are spending something like $12,000 in that place.

For the whole province of Manitoba the estimates only include $5,000.
I will read to the minister a few of the towns in Manitoba and the North-west which are left out in the cold, because the members who represent these constituencies seem to be backward in drawing the attention of the government to the post office revenue derived from them. Boissevan, a growing town, has a post office revenue of $2,651, but we don't hear the member who represents it asking for a post office in that town.
Who is he ?

The Minister of the Interior; he is away. Take the town of Carman, in the county of Lisgar, which has a post office revenue of $3,440, and we are spending nothing there, and the member for Selkirk (Mr. Stewart) does not protest. The town of Deloraine, also in the constituency of the Minister of the Interior, has a revenue of $2,281, and there is no expenditure there. There is the town of Carberry, with a revenue of $3,335, and there is no expenditure there. There is the town of Neepawa, with a revenue of $4,135 and no expenditure ; the town of Selkirk, represented by that stalwart gentleman (Mr. McCreary) has a revenue of $2,193, and there is no expenditure there. The town of Souris, with a revenue of $2,728; the town of Yirden with a post office revenue of $2,926, and also a large revenue from customs, is to have no expenditure. Then we come to Edmonton, in a constituency represented by a supporter of the government; its revenue is $6,039 from the post office, and there is no expenditure In that growing place. It is the same in the town of Lethbridge, which has a revenue of $4,524. The town of Moosejaw, that can scarcely accommodate the immigration flowing in there at the present time, has a post office revenue of $4,427. It is represented by my hon. friend from West Assini-boia (Mr. Scott), and we do not hear a protest from that gentleman because there is no expenditure in that town. It is most unfortunate, Mr. Chairman, that I have to get up to speak of these things. Surely, in the great province of Manitoba and in the Northwest Territories, towards which the eyes of the world are directed now, $5,000 is not sufficient for public buildings, when the little town of L'Assomption with a post office revenue of $465 is to have $10,000 spent on a public building. The town of Prince Al-

bert, represented by another stalwart supporter of the government (Mr. Davis) is to have no expenditure made there. Why do we not hear from him ?
He is building railways.

The town of Yorkton has a revenue of $2,410 and there is no government expenditure there. I could continue to point out, Mr. Chairman, that there are twenty-three post offices in Manitoba with a revenue of from $1,000 to $2,000, and fourteen towns in the North-west Territories with a revenue running from $1,000 to $2,000 that X have said nothing about.
You throw them in.

We will make a job lot of them. Now, Mr. Chairman, I think that the Minister of Public Works, who is a particularly good friend of mine, will admit, that it is most unfortunate that I should be compelled to become the champion of these towns in view of the fact that they are represented by stalwart and outspoken Liberals, who are usually here to speak for themselves if not too embarrassing to the government. I trust that when I come here next year 1 will not have to accuse the Minister of Public Works of neglecting these growing towns.

Sly hon. friend (Mr. Boyd) has referred to the small vote for incidental and unforeseen expenses in the province of Manitoba. Now as a matter of fact there is $12,000 voted for Quebec and Ontario, $12,000 for the maritime provinces, and I think the committee will agree with me that considering the number of buildings in Manitoba the vote of $5,000 is comparatively large. I can assure the hon. gentleman (Mr. Boyd) that the department oyer which I preside could not think of putting up small buildings in the towns he has referred to. In view of the great progress and prosperity of that country, I have no doubt that in a short time they will require very much larger buildings than we would be able to give them at present. They will have due consideration when the time comes.
Valleyfield public buildings, $15,000.
How long is it since this building was determined upon ?
It is two or three years since this vote was first taken.
Is there any correspondence between the local authorities and the department with regard to the selection of the site.
The deputy minister says that he does not remember of any.
Perhaps the ex-Minister of Public Works could give the information. Mr. BOYD.	'

I know Valleyfield very well and before determining on the site I paid a visit to the town. There was practically only one site available. There were other pieces of ground but they were not fit for such a building. The population of Valleyfield is to-day about 15,000, and if things go on as they have been going on within five years it will be a city.
Provided the tariff is alright.
Well, it is to a large extent due to the fact that the tariff on cotton has been kept all right. I may say that I am responsible for the choice of the site.
When was the site decided upon by the department ?

I paid a visit to the place with one of my officers, and chose the site without telling anybody. I then instructed Mr. Dandurand, who is the agent of the Canadian Pacific Railway for land purchases, to purchase the site. Let me say immediately that the site formerly belonged to the sitting member, but it was not bought from him. It was the only site available for a public building there, all other available sites having been bought in the rush of business. I instructed Mr. Dandurand not to say a word to the sitting member, but to take an option on the site. It had been sold previously by the sitting member to a man named Johnston, if I remember rightly. Mr. Dandurand took every possible precaution to secure the site at a reasonable price.
What price did he pay ?
I do not remember exactly ; I lost sight of the transaction. But it was conducted all through by one of the ablest real estate agents in Montreal, and I think everything was done uprightly-
When did Mr. Dandurand close this transaction ?
I think it was closed after I left office. But I gave instructions and was responsible.
The hon. minister might tell us at what date the transaction was closed ?
The Order in Council was passed on the 22nd of November, 1902, authorizing the purchase from R. B. Johnston for the sum of $10,000. The land is 77* feet by 160 feet deep.
The Bank of Hoche-laga has bought a property there which is not worth half as much as this property' and has paid a great deal more. I know we have made a good bargain.

Speaking of this question of sites, I would like to throw out this suggestion. If the policy is to be continued

of giving public buildings to all these small places, at least put the onus upon them of supplying the sites. That will be a buffer between the government and the demand of these small places for public buildings.
I believe it would often have the effect of preventing their construction ; and in cases where it did not, the country would at least be saved the cost of the site.
Who is this R.W. Johnston ? Is he in the employ of the government.
He certainly is not in the employ of the Public Works Department. I am not acquainted with him.
When was the money paid ?
It was paid on the joint order of the agent of the government at Valleyfleld and Mr. R. B. Johnston.
Is it R. B. Johnston or It. W. Johnston ? In the answer given by the minister the other day it was R. W.
The memorandum of the deputy says R. B. Johnston.
When was the money paid ?

The date of the cheque is not stated here. There was some delay in the Department of Justice after the Order in Council was passed ; but so far as the deputy minister can remember, it was about the end of January.

I instructed Mr. Dan-durand to secure the site without the knowledge of the sitting member. I suppose Mr. Dandurand arranged with Mr. Johnston so that he might purchase the site from Mr. Loy without Mr. Loy knowing that it was being purchased for the government. Mr. Dandurand did not let anybody know for whom the site was purchased. All who know Valleyfleld know that my hon. friend could have sold the site at a greater price than we paid. Property is going up there by leaps and bounds.
